battle.title: CAP Clash
battle.description: Pick your side when the network splits: consistency or availability.

questions.text: Which statement about the CAP theorem is correct?
options: When a network partition occurs, a system must trade consistency against availability
A system must permanently give up one of the three properties even on a healthy network
Partition tolerance is optional for systems spanning several data centres
Availability means every piece of data is stored three times
questions.answer: When a network partition occurs, a system must trade consistency against availability
questions.explanation: CAP only forces a choice during a partition: answer possibly stale data (stay available) or refuse some requests (stay consistent). On a healthy network you can have both, and real networks cannot rule out partitions.

questions.text: A bank ledger is replicated across two regions and the link between them fails. Which behaviour is right for transfers?
options: Accept writes on both sides and reconcile later
Accept writes everywhere and drop conflicts silently
Prefer consistency: reject or delay writes that cannot be confirmed by a majority
Take the whole bank offline for every operation
questions.answer: Prefer consistency: reject or delay writes that cannot be confirmed by a majority
questions.explanation: For money, serving a wrong balance or allowing double spending is worse than a temporary refusal, so a CP choice is appropriate. Accepting writes on both sides risks conflicting ledgers.

options: Every read returns the most recent write
Writes are guaranteed never to be lost during a partition
If updates stop, all replicas will converge to the same value
questions.answer: If updates stop, all replicas will converge to the same value
questions.explanation: Eventual consistency allows temporary staleness but guarantees convergence once writes cease. Always seeing the latest write is strong consistency, a much stronger promise.

questions.text: Which guarantee says that once a write is acknowledged, any later read by any client sees that write or a newer one?
questions.explanation: Linearizability applies to all clients. Read-your-writes covers only the client that wrote, and monotonic reads only stops a client from seeing data go backwards in time.

questions.text: Three replicas hold the same key with (timestamp, value) pairs and merge by last-write-wins. What does this program print?
questions.explanation: Last-write-wins keeps the highest timestamp, 12, so value 4 survives and values 7 and 9 are silently discarded. If clocks are skewed, a logically later write can lose, which is why LWW can lose data.
